entries.title: Rethinking Networking in Android (Turning Android Repositories into Composable Effects)
entries.content:
![](https://cdn-images-1.medium.com/max/960/1*08rFY5zR47rSs0XypKNldA.png)

Compose Steps

### The Repository That Forgot Its Purpose

Imagine you are building a feature that needs to fetch a user, create a post on their behalf, upload an attachment, and finally notify them that everything succeeded. In most Android applications, this workflow quickly becomes a chain of repository calls, temporary variables, nested try/catch blocks, and orchestration code spread across use cases or ViewModels. Repositories, despite their name, often become little more than wrappers around Retrofit or Room objects that expose CRUD operations while hiding the implementation details of the underlying data source.

But what if a repository wasn’t a storage abstraction at all? What if, instead of representing *where data comes from*, it represented *a computation that knows how to produce data, propagate failures, and compose with future network operations*? In that world, a repository is no longer a collection of methods like getUser() or createPost(). It becomes a computation that can be transformed, chained, retried, and executed only when needed, allowing complex networking workflows to be expressed as a single, composable pipeline.

This article explores that idea. We’ll rethink the traditional Repository pattern and gradually transform it into an abstraction that carries not only values and failures, but also the networking environment required to continue executing requests. The result is an architecture that eliminates much of the boilerplate surrounding orchestration, centralizes concerns like retries and error handling, and makes networking code read more like a description of a workflow than a sequence of imperative steps.

### What If a Repository Was a Computation?

Before we can transform a repository into a computation, we need to answer a more fundamental question:

> *What exactly is a computation?*

In mathematics, a computation can be thought of as a process that consumes some input, performs a series of transformations, and eventually produces either a value or an error. The details of how that work is performed are often less important than the objects participating in the computation and the rules that govern how they interact.

If we look at a typical networking workflow, three fundamental objects emerge:

1. A value that may succeed or fail.
2. A set of operations that the backend is capable of performing.
3. A mechanism for translating transport-specific data into domain concepts.

Together, these form the foundation upon which the rest of the architecture is built.

#### Values and Failures

Every network request has two possible outcomes: it either succeeds and produces data, or it fails and produces an error.

Instead of representing these possibilities with exceptions, we can model them explicitly using a Result type — specifically, the Result<V, E> from the com.github.michaelbull.result library, which gives us Ok/Err construction plus map/flatMap combinators for free.

```
Result<User, NetworkError>
```

This type tells us that a computation may produce a User, or it may produce a NetworkError.

More importantly, it gives us a predictable structure that can be transformed and composed. Rather than scattering try/catch blocks throughout the application, failure becomes part of the type system itself.

From this perspective, a network request is not a function that returns a value. It is a computation that returns a Result.

#### Capabilities Instead of Endpoints

The second building block is the set of operations available to the computation. Traditional networking layers often expose a large collection of service methods:

```
interface UserService {  
    suspend fun getUser(id: String): UserDto      
    suspend fun createUser(request: CreateUserRequest): UserDto  
}  
  
interface PostService {...}  
  
interface AuthService {...}
```

This approach models the backend in terms of concrete endpoints. Our architecture instead models the backend in terms of capabilities:

```
sealed interface Api  
  
interface Get : Api {  
    suspend fun getUser(id: String): Users.User  
    suspend fun getPosts(): List<Posts.Post>  
}  
  
interface Post : Api {  
    suspend fun createUser(request: UserCreateRequest): Users.User  
    suspend fun createPost(request: PostCreateRequest): Posts.Post  
}  
// Put.kt, Delete.kt, Patch.kt follow the same pattern - and, like Post, extend Api.
```

Notice the subtle difference. The interfaces are no longer describing a particular service implementation. They are describing what operations are possible.

Mathematically, they define the environment in which a computation can execute. A computation that requires Get capability can perform read operations. A computation that requires Post capability can perform write operations. The computation itself does not need to know whether those capabilities are implemented using Retrofit, Ktor, or a test double. It only needs to know that the capability exists.

One naming detail is worth calling out explicitly, because it isn’t obvious until you hit it: Users.User and Posts.Post are qualified on purpose, not for decoration. If you declare interface Post : Api and, elsewhere in the same file or package, a plain data class Post(...) domain model, Kotlin rejects the program outright:

```
error: redeclaration:  
interface Post : Api  
data class Post(val id: String, val title: String)
```

The HTTP-verb capability and the domain noun it eventually returns want the same short name, and only one of them can have it. Wrapping the domain models in small namespacing objects (object Users { data class User(...) }, object Posts { data class Post(...) }) sidesteps the collision entirely and costs nothing at the call site beyond the extra qualifier.

#### Domain Concepts Over Transport Objects

The final building block is the distinction between transport data and business data. Network responses are often shaped by the backend:

```
{  "id": 42,  "name": "John Doe"}
```

These structures exist to satisfy an API contract, not to model the business domain. For that reason, the architecture separates DTOs from domain models.

```
data class UserResponse(val id: Int, val name: String) : DomainModel<Users.User>
```

```
object Users {  
    data class User(val name: String)  
}
```

The DTO is responsible for translating itself into a domain representation:

```
override fun toDomain(): Users.User { return Users.User(name) }
```

This allows every computation to operate on domain concepts rather than transport-specific structures.

As computations are composed together, DTOs disappear and domain models remain.

#### From Objects to Computations

At this point we have all the ingredients necessary to describe a computation:

* A value that may succeed or fail (Result)
* An environment that provides capabilities (Api, Get, Post, ...)
* A way to transform transport data into domain concepts (DomainModel)

What we do not yet have is a way to connect computations together. How does the output of one network request become the input of the next? How do failures automatically short-circuit an entire workflow? How does the networking environment flow through the chain without being passed around explicitly?

To answer those questions, we need one more abstraction: an **effect**.

### The Missing Abstraction: Effects

By themselves, the three building blocks we introduced are not enough to model a networking workflow.

A Result can represent success or failure.

An Api describes the capabilities available to a computation.

A DomainModel translates transport objects into domain concepts.

Yet none of these objects answers a much more interesting question:

> ***How do we describe a computation without executing it?***

Suppose we want to express the following workflow:

```
Fetch User → Create Post → Upload Attachment → Notify User
```

This is more than a sequence of simple function calls. Each step depends on the successful completion of the previous one. Any failure should immediately terminate the workflow; every step requires access to the same networking environment; and yet, nothing should actually execute until we’re ready.

What we need is an object capable of **describing** this computation before it runs. That object is an effect.

### Effects Describe Work

An effect is simply a value that represents work yet to be performed.

Instead of immediately executing a network request, we construct a description of the computation. You might first reach for the simplest possible shape: a computation is just a function from an environment C to a result R.

```
// C represents the environment and R represents the result  
Computation<C, R> ≈ (C) -> R
```

That’s the right intuition, but a bare function type gives us nowhere to hang behaviour — no way to attach compose, no way to attach switchContext. So we wrap it in a class instead, and that class, not the function type above, is what we actually build on for the rest of this piece:

```
class Computation<C, R>(  
    private val f: suspend (C) -> R  
) {  
    suspend fun runInContext(context: C): R =  
        f(context)  
}
```

> *Computation<Get, User> means a computation that requires a* *Get and eventually produces a* *User. The type parameter has been simplified here — normally we'd want a* *Result<User, NetworkError>, not just**User.*

> *An effect separates two ideas:*

> 1. Constructing the computation is one step  
> 2. Executing the computation is another.

This separation gives us something remarkably powerful. Because a computation is now just another value, it can be transformed, combined, passed around, and reasoned about before any network request is ever made.

### Composing Effects

Once computations become values, they can be composed just like any other data structure. Suppose one computation produces a User. A second computation requires that User in order to get the UserHistory. Instead of manually unpacking values and checking for failures, we simply compose the two computations together.

Conceptually, the pipeline looks like this:

```
// we use a simplified representation of a computation.  
(Get) -> User // Given computation_1  
(User) -> (Get) -> UserHistory // computation_2  
(Get) -> UserHistory // producing computation_3
```

A function that composes computation\_1 and computation\_2 can be written as:

```
fun compose(  
    first: (Get) -> User,  
    next: (User) -> (Get) -> UserHistory  
): (Get) -> UserHistory =  
    { get: Get ->  
        next(first(get))(get)  
    }
```

Adapting the compose function for our class, which is generic, we have:

```
class Computation<C, R>(  
    private val f: suspend (C) -> R  
) {  
	fun <R2> compose(  
		f: (R) -> Computation<C,R2>  
	): Computation<C,R2> =  
		Computation { c -> f(this.runInContext(c)).runInContext(c) }  
	  
    suspend fun runInContext(context: C): R =  
        f(context)  
}
```

compose is this codebase's name for what functional programmers usually call flatMap or monadic bind — same operation, domain-specific name. We'll stick with compose consistently from here on, since that's the name the rest of this piece, and the code built on top of it, actually uses.

Now suppose one computation produces a User. A second computation requires that User in order to create a post. We would want to compose both computations, but this yields a new challenge: we change the environment from Get to Post, unlike the first example where the environment is unchanged.

Visualising the pipeline:

```
// we use a simplified representation of a computation.  
(Get) -> User // Given computation_1  
(User) -> (Post) -> Status // computation_2  
(Post) -> Status // producing computation_3
```

Here is the candid truth about changing the environment: because the context is an input to your computation rather than an output, the mapping happens backwards. If we want to create a new computation that accepts a completely different context like Post, we have to provide a function that translates Post back into the Get our original computation actually needs.

```
fun switchContextAndCompose(  
    transform: (Post) -> Get,  
    first: (Get) -> User,  
    next: (User) -> (Post) -> Status  
): (Post) -> Status =  
    { post: Post ->  
        next(first(transform(post)))(post)  
    }
```

It’s worth separating this into two ideas rather than one, because the “switch” half and the “compose” half are independently useful. The switch half — reindexing the environment without touching the result — is the smaller, more primitive operation:

```
class Computation<C, R>(  
    private val f: suspend (C) -> R  
) {  
    fun <R2> compose(  
	f: (R) -> Computation<C,R2>  
    ): Computation<C,R2> =  
	Computation { c -> f(this.runInContext(c)).runInContext(c) }  
  
    // Transforms the Context (Backwards / Contravariant)  
    fun <C2> switchContext(transform: (C2) -> C): Computation<C2, R> =  
        Computation { c2 -> this.runInContext(transform(c2)) }  
  
    // The fused convenience version - switch, then compose, in one call  
    fun <C2, R2> switchContextAndCompose(  
        transform: (C2) -> C,  
        f: (R) -> Computation<C2, R2>  
    ): Computation<C2, R2> =  
        switchContext(transform).compose(f)  
  
    suspend fun runInContext(context: C): R =  
        f(context)  
}
```

switchContextAndCompose isn't hand-written separately from switchContext and compose — it's defined *in terms of* them, and the two forms are provably interchangeable: composing switchContext(transform) with compose(f) produces the exact same result, for any input, as calling switchContextAndCompose(transform, f) directly. Keeping switchContext around as its own method, rather than only ever using the fused version, means a caller who only needs to reindex the environment — without immediately composing anything afterward — has a way to say exactly that, and nothing more.

Each stage consumes the successful result of the previous stage; failures automatically propagate; the networking environment continues to flow through the pipeline.

At this level, we haven’t said anything about Retrofit, Ktor, HTTP clients, retries, logging, or serialization.

The effect only answers one question:

> ***What should happen?***

It deliberately says nothing about **how** it happens.

### Separating Effects from Execution

This distinction eventually led to splitting the architecture into two independent abstractions.

The first is Computation. Its responsibility is to describe computations.

It knows how to:

* compose computations (compose)
* reindex the environment a computation runs against (switchContext)
* propagate failures
* thread the networking environment through the pipeline

It does **not** know how to perform a network request; that responsibility belongs elsewhere.

The second abstraction is NetworkExecutor. Its responsibility is to execute computations.

It decides:

* how requests are dispatched,
* which HTTP client is used,
* whether retries should occur,
* how errors are classified,
* how metrics and logging are collected,
* and how transport-specific exceptions are translated into domain-independent errors.

The effect describes the program.

The executor interprets it.

Mathematically, you can think of the relationship like this:

```
                  Computation  
              (Description of work)  
                       │  
                interpreted by  
                       │  
                NetworkExecutor  
                       │  
        ┌──────────────┴──────────────┐  
        │                             │  
 RetrofitExecutor              KtorExecutor
```

The beauty of this separation is that the description never changes.

Whether the computation is executed using Retrofit, Ktor, a mock implementation, or an in-memory fake for unit tests, the effect remains exactly the same.

Only the interpreter changes.

### From Effects to Programs

At this point, we’ve arrived at a very different understanding of what a repository can be. It is no longer an object that hides a networking library; it is no longer a collection of CRUD methods.

Instead, it becomes a program — a composable description of work that can be folded or reduced, transformed, combined, and laid out as a pipeline.

### Capabilities Instead of Services

Traditional Android architectures typically begin by defining transport scopes named after data domains — such as UserService, PostService, or WeatherService. These traditional definitions explicitly couple your business logic to who owns the endpoint or how the backend team structured their microservices.

A functional, effect-driven architecture turns this inside out. Instead of modelling *ownership scopes*, we model *behavioural capabilities*. The execution framework doesn’t care which service an endpoint belongs to; it only cares about the underlying semantic properties of the HTTP verb being used.

We enforce these properties at the type level using marker interfaces, and — as noted above — every one of them extends Api consistently, since that's what lets a single CapabilityRegistry hold all of them behind one type-safe map:

```
sealed interface Api  
  
interface Get : Api {  
    suspend fun getUser(id: String): Users.User  
    suspend fun getPosts(): List<Posts.Post>  
}  
  
interface Put : Api {  
    suspend fun updateUser(id: String, request: UserUpdateRequest): Users.User  
}  
  
interface Delete : Api {  
    suspend fun deleteUser(id: String)  
}  
  
// Retrying a create can duplicate resources. Do not retry.  
interface Post : Api {  
    suspend fun createUser(request: UserCreateRequest): Users.User  
    suspend fun createPost(request: PostCreateRequest): Posts.Post  
}
```

By splitting capabilities into Get, Post, Put, and Delete, our business logic pipelines depend strictly on behavioural traits.

To centralise these capabilities, we create a CapabilityRegistry class that acts as a service locator by providing a central object from which consumers can dynamically retrieve the service/capability they need by its type, rather than receiving each dependency directly through constructor injection.

```
class CapabilityRegistry internal constructor(  
    @PublishedApi internal val capabilities: Map<KClass<out Api>, Api>  
) {  
  
    inline fun <reified V : Api> get(): V =  
        capabilities[V::class] as? V  
            ?: error("No ${V::class.simpleName} capability registered for this session")  
  
    class Builder {  
        @PublishedApi internal val map = mutableMapOf<KClass<out Api>, Api>()  
        inline fun <reified V : Api> register(instance: V): Builder {  
            map[V::class] = instance  
            return this  
        }  
        fun build(): CapabilityRegistry = CapabilityRegistry(map.toMap())  
    }  
}
```

In the design of this class, we use the builder pattern to separate construction of the registry object from its usage. After construction, consumers get a snapshot rather than a registry that can arbitrarily change underneath them. So, we can increase the number of capabilities of a registry without affecting the portion of code that already uses an instance of this registry.

Things worth noting about the registry:

1. It’s worth being precise about what kind of safety this buys us and what it doesn’t — a .get<V>() call against a registry missing that capability fails at runtime, not compile time. We come back to exactly this trade-off in Correctness by Construction.
2. The registry can contain both low-level transport capabilities like Get, Post, Delete and domain-oriented APIs: UserService, PostService, AuthService if you choose to support the model used by the backend

### Transport Is Just an Interpreter

A major advantage of isolating description from execution is that the pipeline written above remains completely unaware of how the network bytes are delivered. The business logic specifies *what* capabilities it requires, while the concrete implementation of the transport layer is treated merely as an interpreter.

The execution boundary is reduced to a plain suspend interface:

```
interface NetworkExecutor {  
    suspend fun <DTO : DomainModel<Domain>, Domain> execute(  
        retryPolicy: RetryPolicy = RetryPolicy(),  
        request: suspend () -> DTO  
    ): Result<Domain, NetworkError>  
}
```

This design allows you to easily switch between client implementations. Swapping Retrofit out for Ktor requires no modifications to your business logic pipelines or your view models. You simply swap out the concrete interpreter instance provided to the chain.

#### The Retrofit Interpreter

```
import com.github.michaelbull.result.*  
import kotlinx.coroutines.CancellationException  
import kotlinx.coroutines.delay  
import retrofit2.HttpException  
  
class RetrofitExecutor : NetworkExecutor {  
    override suspend fun <DTO : DomainModel<Domain>, Domain> execute(  
        retryPolicy: RetryPolicy,  
        request: suspend () -> DTO  
    ): Result<Domain, NetworkError> {  
        var lastError: NetworkError? = null  
        repeat(retryPolicy.maxRetries) { attempt ->  
            try {  
                return Ok(request().toDomain())  
            } catch (e: CancellationException) {  
                throw e // Must rethrow to respect coroutine structured concurrency  
            } catch (e: HttpException) {  
                val classified = classify(e)  
                if (classified is NetworkError.ServerError && classified.code in retryPolicy.retryableHttpCodes) {  
                    lastError = classified  
                    delay(retryPolicy.delayFor(attempt))  
                } else {  
                    return Err(classified)  
                }  
            } catch (e: Exception) {  
                return Err(NetworkError.Unexpected(e))  
            }  
        }  
        return Err(lastError ?: NetworkError.Unexpected(IllegalStateException("Exhausted retries with no recorded error")))  
    }  
    private fun classify(e: HttpException): NetworkError = when (e.code()) {  
        in 500..599 -> NetworkError.ServerError(e.code(), e)  
        in 400..499 -> NetworkError.ClientError(e.code(), e)  
        else -> NetworkError.Unexpected(e)  
    }  
}
```

#### The Ktor Interpreter

```
import com.github.michaelbull.result.*  
import io.ktor.client.plugins.*  
import kotlinx.coroutines.CancellationException  
import kotlinx.coroutines.delay  
  
class KtorExecutor : NetworkExecutor {  
    override suspend fun <DTO : DomainModel<Domain>, Domain> execute(  
        retryPolicy: RetryPolicy,  
        request: suspend () -> DTO  
    ): Result<Domain, NetworkError> {  
        var lastError: NetworkError? = null  
        repeat(retryPolicy.maxRetries) { attempt ->  
            try {  
                return Ok(request().toDomain())  
            } catch (e: CancellationException) {  
                throw e  
            } catch (e: ServerResponseException) {  
                // Ktor only throws ServerResponseException for 5xx responses in the first  
                // place, so there's no separate "is this eligible" check needed here -  
                // catching this exception type already answers that question.  
                val code = e.response.status.value  
                val classified = NetworkError.ServerError(code, e)  
                if (code in retryPolicy.retryableHttpCodes) {  
                    lastError = classified  
                    delay(retryPolicy.delayFor(attempt))  
                } else {  
                    return Err(classified)  
                }  
            } catch (e: ClientRequestException) {  
                return Err(NetworkError.ClientError(e.response.status.value, e))  
            } catch (e: Exception) {  
                return Err(NetworkError.Unexpected(e))  
            }  
        }  
        return Err(lastError ?: NetworkError.Unexpected(IllegalStateException("Exhausted retries with no recorded error")))  
    }  
}
```

```
import kotlin.random.Random  
  
data class RetryPolicy(  
    val maxRetries: Int = 3,  
    val retryableHttpCodes: Set<Int> = setOf(502, 503, 504),  
    val baseDelayMs: Long = 250L,  
    val maxDelayMs: Long = 4_000L,  
    val jitterMs: Long = 100L  
) {  
    /** Jittered exponential backoff, capped at [maxDelayMs] so retries can't stall forever. */  
    fun delayFor(attempt: Int): Long {  
        val exponential = baseDelayMs * (attempt + 1)  
        val capped = exponential.coerceAtMost(maxDelayMs)  
        return capped + Random.nextLong(0, jitterMs + 1)  
    }  
}
```

### A Real Example: OpenWeather

Everything so far has described Computation in the abstract. Before it's useful, something has to bridge it to NetworkExecutor — nothing yet has shown how a leaf computation actually turns into a real network call. That bridge is a small extension function on NetworkExecutor:

```
fun <C, DTO : DomainModel<Domain>, Domain> NetworkExecutor.effect(  
    retryPolicy: RetryPolicy = RetryPolicy(),  
    request: suspend (C) -> DTO  
): Computation<C, Result<Domain, NetworkError>> =  
    Computation { c -> this.execute(retryPolicy) { request(c) } }
```

Given an executor and a suspend function from the environment to a DTO, effect produces exactly the kind of Computation the rest of this piece has been building toward — one whose result is already a Result<Domain, NetworkError>, with retries and error classification handled by whichever NetworkExecutor you pass in.

With that in place, consider a sequential pipeline where we must first resolve a city’s text name into geographic coordinates before fetching its current weather conditions. Both steps are reads, so both live under the same Get capability:

```
interface Get : Api {  
    suspend fun geocode(city: String): GeoResponseDto  
    suspend fun currentWeather(lat: Double, lon: Double): WeatherResponseDto  
}
```

```
data class Coordinates(val lat: Double, val lon: Double)  
data class GeoResponseDto(val lat: Double, val lon: Double) : DomainModel<Coordinates> {  
    override fun toDomain() = Coordinates(lat, lon)  
}  
data class CurrentWeather(val tempCelsius: Double, val description: String)  
data class WeatherResponseDto(val tempKelvin: Double, val description: String) : DomainModel<CurrentWeather> {  
    override fun toDomain() = CurrentWeather(tempKelvin - 273.15, description)  
}
```

### Composing Network Requests

Because an effect is modelled as a plain immutable value, assembling multiple network requests into an interdependent pipeline becomes highly predictable. Instead of managing complex control flow, developers use combinator functions to transform or chain responses. compose already gets us same-context chaining, but its callback receives the raw R — if R is a Result, compose has no idea it's carrying a Result, and won't stop calling the next step just because the previous one failed. To get that specifically, we build a small, Result-aware layer on top of compose:

```
fun <C, R1, R2, E> Computation<C, Result<R1, E>>.flatMapResult(  
    transform: (R1) -> Computation<C, Result<R2, E>>  
): Computation<C, Result<R2, E>> =  
    this.compose { result: Result<R1, E> ->  
        Computation { c: C ->  
            // Result's own flatMap unwraps on success and short-circuits on  
            // failure, without ever invoking `transform` on the error path.  
            result.flatMap { r1: R1 -> transform(r1).runInContext(c) }  
        }  
    }
```

```
fun <C, R1, R2, E> Computation<C, Result<R1, E>>.mapResult(  
    transform: (R1) -> R2  
): Computation<C, Result<R2, E>> =  
    this.compose { result -> Computation { result.map(transform) } }
```

```
fun <C1, C2, R1, R2, E> Computation<C1, Result<R1, E>>.switchContextAndFlatMapResult(  
    extractContext: (C2) -> C1,  
    transform: (R1) -> Computation<C2, Result<R2, E>>  
): Computation<C2, Result<R2, E>> =  
    this.switchContext(extractContext).flatMapResult(transform)
```

The geocode-then-weather pipeline is a direct application of flatMapResult:

```
fun weatherFor(city: String, executor: NetworkExecutor): Computation<Get, Result<CurrentWeather, NetworkError>> =  
    executor.effect<Get, GeoResponseDto, Coordinates> { get -> get.geocode(city) }  
        .flatMapResult { coordinates ->  
            executor.effect<Get, WeatherResponseDto, CurrentWeather> { get ->  
                get.currentWeather(coordinates.lat, coordinates.lon)  
            }  
        }
```

And running it end to end, through the actual CapabilityRegistry rather than a hand-wired capability instance:

```
val registry = CapabilityRegistry.Builder()  
    .register<Get>(OpenWeatherApi(httpClient))  
    .build()
```

```
val weather: Result<CurrentWeather, NetworkError> =  
    weatherFor("Lagos", RetrofitExecutor()).runInContext(registry.get<Get>())
```

Look closely at what is happening here. Neither .flatMapResult() nor .effect() executes anything eagerly; each call yields a brand-new Computation value that wraps the updated step description. If geocoding fails, the error track instantly short-circuits the rest of the execution — the closure that would call currentWeather is never invoked at all, not merely "unlikely to run." That's not a claim about typical behaviour; it falls directly out of Result.flatMap's definition, which returns immediately on Err without calling its transform.

If this pattern of chaining operations feels familiar, it is because **we have arrived at a Monad**. We did not start with category theory or pure mathematical blueprints; we arrived here entirely out of a practical engineering need to safely compose interdependent, error-prone asynchronous tasks.

The monadic nature of Computation hides the messy infrastructure of Android development behind a clean interface:

* **The Context:** It carries the data state, capability boundaries, and error boundaries along the railway track.
* **The Map Functor:** .mapResult() transforms the success value in place if the pipeline is succeeding, and passes failures through unchanged.
* **The FlatMap/Bind Monad:** .flatMapResult(), and its capability-switching counterpart .switchContextAndFlatMapResult(), each accept a function that takes an unwrapped domain value and produces the next computation — short-circuiting automatically the moment any step in the chain fails.

### Correctness by Construction

Two different kinds of correctness are at play in this architecture, and it’s worth being precise about which parts of the design actually deliver which kind.

**Compile-time.** A Computation<Get, Result<Users.User, NetworkError>> cannot be run against anything that isn't a Get. The type of every computation is a checked claim about what capability it needs — hand it a Post and the program is rejected before it ever runs. Crossing from one capability to another is never silent or implicit; it happens through switchContext, visibly, wherever it occurs in the code. That's the actual return on modelling Get/Post/Put/Delete as marker interfaces rather than as fields on some settings object: not runtime validation, but a program that is simply ill-typed if it tries to use a capability it never declared.

**Runtime, but disciplined.** Whether a particular request succeeds or fails can’t be known until it actually runs — no type signature is going to predict a 500 in advance. What the architecture buys instead is a guarantee about *propagation*. Once flatMapResult composes two steps, a failure in the first is provably incapable of reaching the second: not "the second step will probably be skipped," but literally no code path in flatMapResult's own definition ever invokes the next closure once the first result is an Err. That's a stronger property than "we remembered to check is Err at every call site" — it's checkable directly from the combinator's definition, once, rather than from convention at every place it's used.

**Where this stops being compile-time.** CapabilityRegistry.get<V>() is a runtime lookup. Build a registry that never registered Delete, and something downstream calling .get<Delete>() gets an error(...) at runtime, not a compiler error. This is a deliberate, contained trade-off rather than an oversight — the registry is a single, known point where incomplete configuration becomes a runtime failure, rather than that risk being scattered across arbitrary call sites the way a raw service locator usually allows. It is also, honestly, the one place in this architecture where "correctness by construction" doesn't fully hold. Tightening it further — a registry that only compiles if every capability the workflow's Computation types require was actually registered — is possible, using structurally-typed or phantom-typed registries, but adds real complexity, and isn't a change worth making until a project actually needs it.

### Where This Leaves the Repository Pattern

We started by asking what a repository is actually for, and the traditional answer — “a place that hides where data comes from” — turned out to explain very little about the problems repositories tend to create in practice: orchestration logic bleeding into ViewModels, retry logic copy-pasted across every use case, and no real way to compose two network calls without writing bespoke glue code each time.

The repository doesn’t disappear in this architecture so much as it gets split into pieces that were always doing different jobs. Computation describes what should happen. NetworkExecutor decides how it happens. CapabilityRegistry decides who gets to make it happen. None of the three needs to know how the other two are implemented, and none of them individually resembles a repository — which is the point. What used to be a UserRepository with six unrelated methods on it becomes a handful of small, independently testable Computation values, composed together at the point a feature actually needs them, rather than pre-bundled into a class organised around a database table or a REST resource that has nothing to do with how the app actually uses it.

The cost is real, and worth naming plainly: this is more machinery than a repository interface and an implementation. For a small app with three network calls that never compose, it’s almost certainly overkill. It earns its complexity specifically where the original problem lived — workflows that chain several requests, need consistent retry and error handling across all of them, and where “does this actually short-circuit on failure” used to be true only because someone remembered to write if (result is Err) return at every step. Here, it's true because the composition operators don't have another code path to take.

![](https://medium.com/_/stat?event=post.clientViewed&referrerSource=full_rss&postId=3e9310687a8b)

---

[Rethinking Networking in Android (Turning Android Repositories into Composable Effects)](https://proandroiddev.com/rethinking-networking-in-android-turning-android-repositories-into-composable-effects-3e9310687a8b) was originally published in [ProAndroidDev](https://proandroiddev.com) on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

entries.title: From AI Copilots to Agent Swarms
entries.content:
![](https://spectrum.ieee.org/media-library/colorful-3d-blocks-piled-behind-glass-panels-displaying-white-code-snippets.jpg?id=67609515&width=1245&height=700&coordinates=0%2C187%2C0%2C188)  
  

The impact of AI on software development has been both profound and ever-evolving. Last year, I [wrote](https://spectrum.ieee.org/beyond-code-autocomplete) about [AMD’s](https://www.amd.com/en.html) plans to use AI not just for [generating](https://spectrum.ieee.org/best-ai-coding-tools) new lines of code, but also for other steps in the software development lifecycle (SDLC), such as triaging problems, debugging code, and testing the software. At the time, we were hoping for a 25 percent productivity boost from AI use over the course of two or three years.

But with each new release, the capabilities of Large Language Models (LLMs) improve dramatically—accelerating software development, increasing the quality of AI-generated code, and fundamentally reshaping how software is engineered. Now, just one year later, we have surpassed our productivity target, achieving a 30 percent overall productivity boost through AI. On top of that, we are rethinking not only how we use AI within the SDLC, but the structure of the SDLC itself.

We believe that the biggest AI revolution in software engineering is still ahead. So far, we have largely been teaching AI how we perform tasks and asking it to mimic existing workflows. In many ways, this constrains AI to human patterns of thinking. The next transformation will come from collaborative swarms of AI agents capable of discovering solutions independently.

## Agents of today

AMD began developing AI systems for code generation, testing automation, bug analysis, and code review in 2024. At the time, our objective was to achieve 25 percent AI-generated production code by 2027 while gradually automating larger portions of the SDLC.

Measuring productivity is inherently [challenging](https://metr.org/blog/2025-07-10-early-2025-ai-experienced-os-dev-study/), but from the outset we have consistently tracked one objective metric: the percentage of source code generated by AI. Importantly, we count only code that passes all reviews and testing and is ultimately included in the final product. While AI-generated code is certainly not the only contributor to productivity gains, it is one of the few metrics that can be measured objectively and consistently.

By this metric, we have crossed the 20 percent mark at the beginning of this year and are now progressing toward 50 percent across entire codebase. In some software components, more than 80 percent of the code is now generated using AI.

Agentic AI has enabled us to include AI in every step of the lifecycle: For **code analysis and triage**, agents are trained to analyze problem reports, identify and group similar requests, and highlight which code snippets are likely to need modification. For **debugging and code generation**, agents are directed to analyze a bug request and implement required code changes. For **testing**, the agents generate unit tests, and if those are passed, identify necessary integration and product-level tests. And finally, for the **approval and release** stage, agents prepare architecture summary, code change review and full test results for engineers’ review and approval and if approved, integrate the changes into the next release.

## Agents of tomorrow

Today, engineers create AI agents in their own image: they teach AI what they know about the system, how they would fix an issue, and how they would implement a change. This is already a major technological advancement. Engineers can create multiple “AI versions” of themselves, allowing these agents to work in parallel, scaling their expertise far beyond the limits of individual productivity. The limitation, however, is that these AI agents are still constrained by human thinking and human-defined approaches.

![Person typing on a keyboard. Looming in front of them is a network of colorful AI agents surrounding a glowing central node.](https://spectrum.ieee.org/media-library/person-typing-on-a-keyboard-looming-in-front-of-them-is-a-network-of-colorful-ai-agents-surrounding-a-glowing-central-node.jpg?id=67609528&width=980) AMD

We believe the next major transformation in software engineering will occur when collaborative AI agent swarms can independently identify and develop solutions, guided by humans on what to solve rather than constrained by human assumptions about how the job should be done. Instead of providing detailed instructions on how to solve a problem, engineers will define the issue, the desired outcome and the quality, performance, and system constraints allowing AI agents to determine the optimal path to a solution.

A swarm of AI agents will then work in parallel to generate, evaluate, and refine multiple solution approaches. These agents will automatically validate correctness, measure performance, test trade-offs, and compare alternative implementations against defined success criteria. Finally, AI agents will prepare ranked solution options, along with validation results and performance metrics, for engineer review and approval. The agents won’t be enhancing each step of the SDLC—they will be rewriting the SLDC themselves.

To get to this point, we need to change how agents are trained. Today, improvement occurs one engineer and one agent at a time: an engineer reviews the output, refines the prompt, and repeats the process. To scale beyond this model, agents must continuously learn from one another, reuse successful strategies, and improve collaboratively across projects and teams.

We are already moving in this direction by using multi-agent workflows extensively through agentic harnesses, such as Codex and Claude Code, while simultaneously developing our own internal multi-agent systems to support the next generation of AI-driven software engineering.

A good example is our AI-driven effort to resolve issues in our Radeon Software eXperience (RSX). RSX is a user interface component that allows users to configure and monitor graphics driver behavior. In October 2025, we began using AI agents to automatically debug and fix reported RSX issues. Out-of-the-box AI tools delivered limited results, resolving only 6% of issues.

![A bar chart labelled RSX-Agentic Resolution Rate shows large percentage increases from 6 in October 2025 to 75 in June 2026.](https://spectrum.ieee.org/media-library/a-bar-chart-labelled-rsx-agentic-resolution-rate-shows-large-percentage-increases-from-6-in-october-2025-to-75-in-june-2026.jpg?id=67609523&width=980) The percentage of software issues fixed automatically by AI agents in AMD’s Radeon Software eXperience (RSX) has been growing steadily, reaching 75 percent in June 2026.

As we analyzed failures and identified ways to improve, we built a learning loop—initially a largely manual process—to understand where the agents were falling short and how to improve them. Rather than retraining the underlying models, we refined the objectives given to the agents, allowing them to iteratively explore multiple approaches, evaluate the results against defined success criteria, and converge on better solutions. At the same time, advances in models and agent runtimes further increased effectiveness. Together, these improvements significantly increased our resolution rate from 6 percent to more than 75 percent of RSX issues resolved by agentic loop.

To make agents and agent swarms truly productive, we need a continuous learning loop that feeds errors and human interventions back into future agent workflows. The opportunity is to engineer this loop around clear, measurable goals. Each cycle captures new insights, making the entire AI engineering workflow smarter and more effective. Over time, this self-reinforcing loop—not just the underlying model—will become a key driver of AI progress.

## The evolving role of human engineers

At AMD, we view AI as a means of increasing productivity, improving quality, and enabling employees to focus on higher-value work. Our goal is to empower our workforce with AI, not to reduce headcount.

To support this transformation, we are investing heavily in AI education and training across the company. The way we work is evolving rapidly, and we want every AMD employee to be prepared to leverage AI confidently, responsibly, and effectively.

As AI agents continue to improve, engineers will spend less time manually implementing solutions, focusing more on defining specifications, validating outcomes, and making the strategic decisions that drive innovation.

entries.title: Danish town plans for underground parking garage, finds long-lost medieval convent
entries.content:
Archaeologists in Denmark have finally pinpointed the remnants of a long lost [13th-century monastery](https://www.popsci.com/science/medieval-shipwreck-rubbish-england/), although its location may dismay local sports fans. With the help of ground-penetrating radar (GPR), researchers confirmed that traces of St. Clare’s Convent still exist roughly six feet beneath a soccer field in the town of Roskilde west of Copenhagen.

“We knew that St. Clare’s Convent had been located here, but not how much of the complex from 1256 [CE] had been preserved,” Jesper Langkilde, an archeologist at the [Roskilde Museum](https://romu.dk/) (ROMU) recently told the [Norwegian Institute for Cultural Heritage Research](https://www.niku.no/en/2026/08/thought-the-monastery-was-lost-found-the-entire-complex-with-ground-penetrating-radar-under-a-football-pitch/).

Roskilde served as a religious and royal power hub during the [Middle Ages](https://www.popsci.com/science/medieval-knight-stories-lost-to-time/). By the 16th century, the Protestant Reformation ushered in the dissolution of many local Catholic institutions, and St. Clare itself was demolished. As a result, over half a million bricks from the convent were used in construction projects at the nearby Selsø Castle. Many historians long assumed that little—if any—of the convent still existed, leaving a major gap in researchers’ understanding of the era’s monastic architecture.

That may soon change due to local plans for an underground parking garage. Although the initial goal was to construct the facility beneath Roksilde’s soccer field, Danish officials and preservationists first wanted to complete a subterranean survey to ensure that any undocumented historical remnants were not disturbed. Langkilde and colleagues at ROMU collaborated with the National Museum of Denmark and the Norwegian Institute for Cultural Heritage Research (NIKU) to oversee underground scans of the surrounding land.

GPR emits electromagnetic waves capable of penetrating the soil beneath it. These waves then bounce off any objects or structures containing different materials like stone, brickwork, or other human remnants. This data is then processed into visual maps. Although GPR often offers striking details, archaeologists were particularly surprised by what it could detect in Roksilde.

“The results are simply impressive. GPR data do not always provide such clear images, and often the interpretation requires extensive analytical work,” explained NIKU archaeologist Arne Abel Stamnes.

He recalled being able to discern structures in real-time while driving across the soccer field.

“In my assessment these are among the clearest GPR results from a monastery complex in Scandinavia,” he added.

GPR mapping highlighted parts of the building including cloisters, room dividers, a church, and a particularly well-preserved eastern wing featuring more walls and vaulting pillars. The data also suggests the existence of multiple external buildings and structures outside the main monastery square.

The discoveries complicate municipal matters, however. Roskilde’s four other medieval monasteries are mapped and legally protected, but the soccer field above St. Clare’s is not due to the assumption that nothing of the convent remained. Moving forward, archaeologists will begin preliminary excavation work to further assess the centuries’ old structures. From there, it will be up to both historians and local authorities to determine the best path forward—although it’s safe to assume parking garage plans are currently on hold.

The post [Danish town plans for underground parking garage, finds long-lost medieval convent](https://www.popsci.com/science/convent-soccer-field-denmark/) appeared first on [Popular Science](https://www.popsci.com).

entries.title: Meet the only known trebuchet casualty in history
entries.content:
During a medieval siege, a trebuchet scored a chance hit one unlucky defender. A small boulder slammed into his upper back at close to 300 kilometers an hour, smashing bones and crushing him beneath its weight.

The man’s skeleton lay beneath the chapel of Scotland’s Stirling Castle, along with the remains of several other people who had clearly died violent deaths. But this one, known to us only as Skeleton 150 (or as “trebuchet guy” in your faithful correspondent’s notes), stood out even among that battle-damaged crowd because most of his upper body had been shattered. According to University of Bradford paleopathologist Jo Buckberry, who [presented her research](https://cfp.dainst.org/25th-european-ppa-meeting/talk/GHF9V8/) at the 25th European Meeting of the Paleopathology Association last week, skeleton 150 is the only known trebuchet casualty in history.

## A shattered skeleton

Skeleton 150 was in terrible shape, even for a dead guy. The man’s skull had broken in 61 separate places, and another 60 jagged bits of bone were distributed across his ribs. His right shoulder was broken, and his right leg above the knee was basically shattered.

[Read full article](https://arstechnica.com/science/2026/08/meet-the-only-known-trebuchet-casualty-in-history/)

[Comments](https://arstechnica.com/science/2026/08/meet-the-only-known-trebuchet-casualty-in-history/#comments)

entries.title: Klibs.io Grows to 4,200+ KMP Projects With Smarter Discovery and New AI Integrations
entries.source: Kotlin : A concise multiplatform language developed by JetBrains | The JetBrains Blog
entries.content:
Explore a growing Kotlin Multiplatform catalog in your browser, or bring up-to-date library data directly into your AI development workflow through the klibs.io MCP server.  
  
When we [introduced klibs.io in December 2024](https://blog.jetbrains.com/kotlin/2024/12/introducing-klibs-io-a-new-way-to-discover-kotlin-multiplatform-libraries/), the goal was simple: make it easier to find a Kotlin Multiplatform library that fits both your use case and target platforms. Since then, klibs.io has grown into a catalog of more than 4,200 KMP projects – and discovering new libraries has become even easier.

[Explore Kotlin Multiplatform projects on klibs.io](https://klibs.io/ "Explore Kotlin Multiplatform projects on klibs.io")

## **Discover more than 4,200+ KMP projects**

klibs.io combines information from GitHub and Maven Central, bringing the details needed to evaluate a project into a single catalog. When source metadata is incomplete, klibs.io uses LLMs to refine descriptions and tags, improving search and discoverability.

![](https://blog.jetbrains.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/klibsio-4200-projects-by-tags.png)

Discovery now goes well beyond a basic keyword search. Use multiple search terms, filter by supported platforms and targets – including Android, iOS, JVM, JavaScript, and Wasm – and browse curated categories such as Compose UI, local storage, networking, or dependency injection. Results can be sorted by relevance, GitHub stars, or dependent count.

Project pages make comparison easier by bringing together descriptions, tags, `README` content, supported platforms, package versions, dependent counts, license information, and project activity.

This gives you a clearer view of whether a library fits your project before you add the dependency.

**TIP:**
Explore klibs.io’s
[Grant winners](https://klibs.io/?category=grant-winners)
category – KMP libraries recognized by the Kotlin Foundation Grants Program for their quality and impact.

## **Bring klibs.io into your AI workflow**

Library decisions often happen while you are already coding. The new AI integrations allow coding agents to pull structured, up-to-date data from klibs.io rather than relying solely on training data or a general web search.

### **Connect through the klibs.io MCP server**

The [klibs.io MCP server](https://github.com/JetBrains/klibs-io/tree/master/integrations/mcp#readme) lets agents search Kotlin Multiplatform projects by platform and target and retrieve the latest published package versions directly from the klibs.io index.

### **Give agents reusable KMP library expertise**

The [Kotlin Multiplatform Libraries expert skill](https://klibs.io/ai#skill) provides task-specific instructions for discovering and comparing libraries, recommending options for a use case, verifying platform support, and finding up-to-date dependency coordinates and stable versions. We measured agent output with and without klibs.io connected – the [evaluation results](https://github.com/JetBrains/klibs-io/blob/f42d394e3b1a18757193241386aec7753437dc62/mcp-eval/RESULTS.md) are published in the klibs.io repository.

### **Keep project guidance close to the code**

The [AI integration guide](https://klibs.io/ai#overview) includes setup instructions and a [recommended AGENTS.md snippet](https://klibs.io/ai#agents). Adding guidance to a project helps AI tools consistently use verified information from the KMP library.

[Explore AI development with klibs.io](https://klibs.io/ai#overview "Explore AI development with klibs.io")

## **Help shape what comes next**

klibs.io is an open-source project, and feedback from library users and authors helps the catalog keep improving. Here are a few ways to take part:

•  **Try it out:** Search for a library, explore a category, and see how the filters work for your target platforms.

•  **Improve project information:** Project owners can use the *Suggest an edit* option on project pages to propose better descriptions and tags through GitHub.

•  **Report issues or contribute:** Report bugs, missing libraries, or incorrect metadata in the [GitHub issue tracker](https://github.com/JetBrains/klibs-io/issues/new/choose), or contribute directly to the [open-source project](https://github.com/JetBrains/klibs-io).

•  **Join the discussion:** Share feedback in the [#klibs-io channel on Kotlin Slack](https://kotlinlang.slack.com/archives/C081AF4JK70).

Whether you browse the catalog directly or integrate it with your AI tools, klibs.io now makes it easier to discover, compare, and use Kotlin Multiplatform libraries with up-to-date information.

entries.title: GitHub Is Down
entries.content:
If you're trying (and failing) to access GitHub Monday morning, you aren't alone. [According to Downdetector](https://downdetector.com/status/github/ "open in a new window"), the hosting provider has over 3,000 user reports indicating issues or downtime with the service. Whether you're a developer trying to update your repository, or you're a user trying to access one, GitHub may give you trouble.

If the comments on Downdetector are any indication, this is not the first time GitHub has had service issues. One comment reads: "Cmon [GitHub] get your sh\*t together...this is getting old." (The user added their own asterisks.) Scrolling through the comment history, users reported errors one or twice a week throughout August. I'm not a regular GitHub user, so I can't attest personally to repeated downtimes, but it does seem as though this isn't wholly unusual.

As such, even though it isn't clear why GitHub is down right now, chances are good that the company will get the site up and running shortly. Assuming nothing catastrophic is happening behind the scenes, developers and users alike should be able to access the site sometime today. But I will continue to update this piece if GitHub's downtime extends longer than normal.

entries.title: OpenAI Ditches Recall-Style Screenshot Surveillance For Friendly Keylogging
entries.content:
An anonymous reader quotes a report from The Register: If you want to record whatever you do on a computer, send those records to OpenAI, use more ChatGPT tokens, and increase your vulnerability to prompt injection, then OpenAI has something for you. It's called Computer History, an opt-in way to record your computer interactions across apps and websites as memories organized on a timeline.
Why would you want to do so? Maybe you found Chronicle, the predecessor of Computer History which compiled similar histories using screenshots, a bit too intrusive but don't mind Computer History's approach -- recording input events and storing them unencrypted locally for 48 hours (or more), with a brief visit to OpenAI's servers. Maybe you're not bothered by the warning OpenAI includes in its documentation: "Computer History files can contain sensitive information. They are not encrypted by Computer History, and other programs running as your macOS user may be able to access them."
Perhaps, having given OpenAI's Codex and GPT Work the run of your computer, you're already sold on the suggestion that storing your computer activity in memory files and arranging those interactions in a timeline will improve ChatGPT responses, surface opportunities for automation, and make it easier to resume prior work. Computer History is, to put it bluntly, a keylogging and event capture system. "Computer History creates an interaction-event stream from allowed apps and websites," OpenAI's documentation explains. "Events can include clicks, typing, keyboard shortcuts, app switches, and context that macOS exposes through its accessibility system. Computer History periodically turns these events into text summaries and local memory files." OpenAI says the feature doesn't capture screen images, microphone input, or system audio. It also doesn't record private-mode browsing.
"Turn it off during communications with other people unless you have their prior express consent," the company advises, perhaps in acknowledgement of legal risk. "Consider pausing it or excluding apps that contain sensitive health, financial, or personal information." ChatGPT and Codex delete locally stored Computer History interaction events after 48 hours, but data sent to OpenAI to generate memories may be retained locally longer and reused in future chats.

[![](https://a.fsdn.com/sd/twitter_icon_large.png)](http://twitter.com/home?status=OpenAI+Ditches+Recall-Style+Screenshot+Surveillance+For+Friendly+Keylogging%3A+https%3A%2F%2Fyro.slashdot.org%2Fstory%2F26%2F08%2F17%2F0454255%2F%3Futm_source%3Dtwitter%26utm_medium%3Dtwitter)

entries.title: Mole 1.12.1 一站式隐私安全型 macOS 系统清理与维护专家
entries.content:
![](https://img.xclient.info/attachment/2026/07/8e47e77d-04d5-a803-27c7-f3326d703197.png)

## 应用介绍

**Mole** 是一款将清理、卸载、性能优化、磁盘分析及系统健康监测融为一体的综合性 macOS 系统管理工具。它通过单一应用整合了碎片化的维护功能，并以“本地安全与绝对透明”为核心设计策略。

#### 核心功能

* **保守型本地安全机制**：
  + **隐私防护**：所有扫描与清理作业均完全在本地执行，严禁向网络上传文件内容或浏览历史。
  + **操作确认**：执行清理前，系统必须显式列出目标文件明细及所占空间，由用户手动确认后方可触发执行。
  + **风险规避**：支持通过“全盘访问权限（Full Disk Access）”进行深度扫描，但在遭遇不确定或可疑系统项目时会自动跳过，避免破坏系统文件。
* **多维度系统清理与卸载**：
  + 支持清除系统缓存、运行时日志及各类临时文件。
  + 精准检测并移除应用程序卸载后的残留垃圾，以及从 Dock 栏中清理失效的启动项。
* **磁盘空间大图分析**：内置树状图（Tree Map）分析功能，将庞杂的磁盘目录可视化，帮助用户一眼识别出占用空间巨大的“大文件”。
* **全方位硬件实时监测**：集成硬件监控面板，提供 CPU、内存、GPU、磁盘、网络、电池以及设备温度等各项核心硬件指标的实时数据反馈。

entries.title: JEP 540 Proposed to Target JDK 28 with a Simple JSON API
entries.content:
![](https://res.infoq.com/news/2026/08/java-native-json-api/en/headerimage/generatedHeaderImage-1786934139615.jpg)

JEP 540, Simple JSON API, has progressed to Target status for JDK 28. It introduces a compact API for parsing and generating JSON documents without external dependencies. Focused on core tasks, it provides an immutable value hierarchy. The API allows simple traversal and conversion while enforcing strict syntax rules. Feedback during incubation will shape its future development.

*By A N M Bazlur Rahman*

entries.title: Who gets credit when AI joins the team? Rethinking what it means to own an idea
entries.content: A few months ago, AI made headlines for cracking a mathematical puzzle that had stumped experts for decades. Mathematician Paul Erdős posed the unit-distance conjecture, predicting how many pairs of points could lie the same distance apart. AI proved it wrong by tracking down a group of infinite counterexamples to the solution Erdős proposed.
